status_reason: The client asks whether the study proves readiness for surgical decisions; it does not, and use on patients needs validation beyond a first assessment.
answer: The kidney study cannot be quoted as proof that the sensor is ready for tumor-boundary decisions in live surgery. It is an in vitro proof of concept on 14 samples from 7 patients, with very high variance in cancer tissue and much work remaining. The sensible next step is laboratory testing of NIR on matched tissue samples, with independent histology as reference, before any surgical use.

inline.headline: Test NIR diffuse reflection in a laboratory set-up on kidney tumor and normal samples before any surgical use
inline.install: laboratory measurement on tissue samples, not in the operating room
inline.test_against: MIR ATR probe on the same samples
inline.not_final_because: The only kidney study is an in vitro proof of concept with very high variance and no in vivo data, and the NIR range of 780-2500 nm extends beyond the listed silica fiber range of 350-2400 nm.

problems.text: The kidney study is not proof of surgical readiness. It tested two prototypes on 14 in vitro samples from 7 patients, measured thawed frozen biopsies, and the authors call it a proof of concept with very high variance and unacceptable false negatives.

The study can be quoted only as an in vitro proof of concept that an LED NIR sensor captured tumor-related variance in kidney samples. The surgical concept is an application idea with no validation data, and neither applies to another sensor, organ or set-up without new data.
Spectral range: the NIR method is listed at 780-2500 nm, but the silica Vis-NIR fiber covers 350-2400 nm, so the top end is not covered. The kidney study used LEDs at 900-1500 nm.

Sensor set-up: the kidney study used only four LEDs, the authors say the LED set must be adapted to each tissue and cancer type, and probe construction needs optimisation. The client has no validation on its own setup.

methods.why: It is the only method used on kidney tissue in the supplied study; NIR penetrates about 3 mm of tissue and suits remote fiber probes, but this sensor set-up still needs its own validation.
The combined tumor-boundary work used MIR ATR with fluorescence, and ATR probes suit liquids and soft solids, but MIR is limited to very thin layers.
It is highly sensitive, but most chemicals do not fluoresce and the approach needs a fluorescent component in the sample.
It is complementary to MIR, but fluorescence can mask its weak signals and it needs special probes.

experiment.objective: Test whether NIR on matched kidney tumor and normal samples separates the classes, with independent histology as reference, before any surgical use.
steps: Obtain matched tumor and normal tissue samples with independent histology as reference, recording the patient ID for each sample.
Measure each sample at several points with a NIR diffuse reflection probe over the study band of 900-1500 nm and the full NIR range.
Record the same points with a MIR ATR probe if available, checking that both probes sample the same spot.
Build PLS-DA or PCA models with patient-based segmented cross-validation and randomisation tests.
Compare the NIR model with the MIR ATR and fused models on the same validation data, and review the result before any in vivo planning.
experiment.go_no_go: Criteria come from the client: accuracy, specificity and false-negative limits set before testing.

pathway.key_features: No spectral analysis was supplied; key features must come from lab spectra, starting from the 900-1500 nm band used in the kidney study.
pathway.path_reason: Surgical use is outside supported scope and the lab test has not been done.

multispectral.why: NIR reaches several millimetres into tissue with broad overlapping bands, while MIR gives well-defined absorption peaks, so the information is complementary; the tumor-boundary work found NIR+IR beneficial.
multispectral.test: Compare the fused model with the best single method on the same patient-split validation data; the combination is only a hypothesis until it beats the NIR model, and both probes must sample the same spot.

assumptions: The proposed sensor is assumed to be an LED-based NIR sensor like the kidney study's.
The target is the kidney tumor boundary, as the enquiry suggests.
Lab samples are assumed to be ex vivo tissue, not in vivo.
